title: Module Declarations & File Organization (C++20/23/26)
summary: Primary module interfaces, module implementation units, and private module fragments for organizing modular code.
rules: Every module has exactly one primary module interface unit declared with 'export module <name>;'.
Module implementation units use 'module <name>;' without 'export' and do not export symbols.
Use private module fragment ('module :private;') only in primary interface units when no other implementation units exist.
Functions defined inside a module purview do not require 'inline' to prevent ODR violations.
All definitions exported by a module must be part of the interface purview.

title: Standard Library Modules: import std and import std.compat (C++23/C++26)
summary: Importing the standard library via 'import std;' vs 'import std.compat;', performance gains, and compiler support.
rules: Use 'import std;' in C++23+ for standard library symbols in the 'std' namespace.
Use 'import std.compat;' only if you need C standard library functions in the global namespace (e.g. '::printf').
Never mix '#include <vector>' and 'import std;' in the same translation unit without a global module fragment.
'import std;' provides 5x-10x faster compilation compared to including all heavy headers (<algorithm>, <ranges>, <iostream>).
Macros like 'assert' or 'errno' are NOT exported by 'import std;'; include <cassert> in the global module fragment if needed.

title: Module Partitions: Architecture & Cyclic Dependencies (C++20/23/26)
summary: Splitting complex modules into interface partitions and internal implementation partitions without exposing internal structure to users.
rules: Interface partitions ('export module A:B;') must be re-exported by the primary interface with 'export import :B;'.
Internal partitions ('module A:Internal;') are visible only within module A and CANNOT be exported.
Partitions cannot have cyclic dependencies between each other.
External consumers only import the primary module ('import A;'), never individual partitions ('import A:B;' is illegal for consumers).
Use partitions instead of multiple separate modules when classes or functions share an internal implementation contract.

title: Global Module Fragment & Legacy Header Hygiene
summary: Using 'module;' to include third-party or legacy headers, avoiding macro leakage, and preventing ODR violations.
rules: The global module fragment MUST appear first in the file with 'module;' before 'export module <name>;'.
Only preprocessor directives (#include, #define, #ifdef) are permitted inside the global module fragment.
Never put '#include' inside the module purview (after 'export module'); put all '#include's in the global module fragment.
Macros defined in headers inside the global module fragment are active only in that translation unit and are NOT exported.
Symbols from headers in the global module fragment are not automatically exported unless explicitly 'export'ed.

title: Module Linkage, Visibility vs Reachability, and ODR (C++20/23/26)
summary: Module linkage, how visibility differs from reachability, and why 'inline' is no longer required for ODR in module purviews.
rules: Symbols declared in a module without 'export' have 'module linkage' (visible across all units of that module, invisible outside).
Functions defined in a module interface do NOT need 'inline' to avoid Multiple Definition errors.
A type can be 'reachable' even if it is not 'visible' (e.g. returned by an exported function without the type itself being exported).
Do not return unexported types from exported functions unless deliberately designing an opaque handle.
Templates defined in a module interface must have their complete definition in the interface unit.

title: CMake 3.28+ Native C++ Modules & Ninja Build Configuration
summary: Configuring CMake 3.28+ with FILE_SET CXX_MODULES, Ninja generator, and compiler flags for GCC, Clang, and MSVC.
rules: Use CMake 3.28 or later; earlier CMake versions do not support standard C++20 modules reliably.
Always use the 'Ninja' generator or Visual Studio 2022 Generator; standard Unix Makefiles do NOT support C++ module scanning.
Declare module interfaces using 'target_sources(target PUBLIC FILE_SET CXX_MODULES FILES ...)'.
For C++23 'import std;', set 'set(CMAKE_CXX_MODULE_STD ON)' in CMake 3.30+ or use compiler-specific std modules.
Do not manually craft compilation commands for BMIs; let CMake and Ninja handle module dependency scanning (P1689R5).
content:
### Idiomatic `CMakeLists.txt` for C++20/C++23 Modules

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.28)
project(ModularCppApp LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

# Required for building with C++20 modules
# Generator MUST be Ninja: cmake -B build -G Ninja

# 1. Define modular library
add_library(core_lib)
target_sources(core_lib
    PUBLIC
        FILE_SET CXX_MODULES FILES
            src/core.cppm
            src/core_math.cppm
    PRIVATE
        src/core_impl.cpp
)

# 2. Define application using the modular library
add_executable(app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core_lib)
```

### C++23 `import std;` in CMake 3.30+

```cmake
# Enable standard library modules in CMake 3.30+
set(CMAKE_EXPERIMENTAL_CXX_IMPORT_STD "0e5b6991-d74f-473d-941e-73b8437c3b24")
set(CMAKE_CXX_MODULE_STD ON)

add_executable(my_app src/main.cpp)
# Now 'import std;' works seamlessly in GCC 14, Clang 18, and MSVC 19.36+
```

### Recommended File Extensions
- `.cppm`: Standard-agnostic preferred extension for module interfaces.
- `.ixx`: Default module interface extension for MSVC.
- `.cpp` / `.cc`: Module implementation units.

title: Migrating from Headers to Modules: Dual-Mode & Façade Strategies
summary: Step-by-step strategies for transitioning large C++ codebases to modules without breaking non-modular consumers.
rules: Do not rewrite the entire codebase at once; start by modularizing bottom-level leaf utilities (math, string utils, logging).
Use the 'Module Wrapper / Façade' pattern to expose existing headers via modules immediately.
Use Dual-Mode macros when a library must be consumable both via '#include' and 'import' simultaneously.
Ensure all third-party dependencies are included in the global module fragment during transition.
Verify that transitive header dependencies are cleanly replaced by module imports.

title: Top Modules Pitfalls, Anti-Patterns, and Debugging Techniques
summary: Common mistakes with C++ modules, leaky reachability, header pollution, circular partition references, and compiler diagnostic troubleshooting.
rules: Anti-Pattern 1: Leaking unexported dependent types (creates compiler errors in downstream template instantiations).
Anti-Pattern 2: Macro pollution in module purview (always quarantine macros in 'module;').
Anti-Pattern 3: Circular partition imports (split shared interfaces into a separate partition).
Anti-Pattern 4: Defining static data members with internal linkage in module interfaces.
Anti-Pattern 5: Expecting '#define' flags from importer to alter module behavior (modules are precompiled and isolated from importer macros).

title: C++26 Modules Evolution & Next-Gen Standard Features
summary: How C++26 enhances modules: reflection interaction, contract assertions across module interfaces, and standard library completions.
rules: In C++26, Contracts (P2900R6) assertions on exported module functions become part of the module interface contract.
Compile-time Reflection (P2996R5) operates across module boundaries with zero macro overhead.
C++26 expands standard library modularization to ensure full coverage of freetime math, numerics, and SIMD.
Binary Module Interface caching and distributed compilation protocols are standardized in toolchain ecosystems.
